system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2127-06-21 21:39:00 to 2127-06-24 18:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, tracheostomy, and PEG dependence was admitted from a skilled nursing facility for fever and vomiting. Workup revealed a vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus urinary tract infection and possible aspiration-related pneumonia. He was treated with linezolid for the VRE UTI and cefepime for the lung infection, with clinical improvement. A CT scan showed bladder wall thickening and diverticula, raising concern for chronic urinary retention; a Foley catheter was placed as he did not tolerate intermittent catheterization, and outpatient urodynamic testing was scheduled. A pressure- and moisture-related rash on the back was treated with topical steroids and antifungal powder. He completed a 7-day antibiotic course, remained stable, and was discharged to extended care with instructions to continue oral vancomycin for C. diff prophylaxis, maintain the Foley catheter until urology follow-up, and resume all chronic medications including antiretrovirals and seizure prophylaxis.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Enterococcus as the cause of diseases classified elsewhere
Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food and vomit
Chronic respiratory failure, unspecified whether with hypoxia or hypercapnia
Rash and other nonspecific skin eruption

procedures.long_title: Change Feeding Device in Upper Intestinal Tract, External Approach

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospital doctors. You're at the medical center now after your feeding tube clogged at the nursing home. Do you remember coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… little confused. Tube… not working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. The team in the ER changed the outer part of the tube and got it flushing again. No need to replace the whole tube. You’re stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good… hungry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know you’re used to tube feeds, but we held them briefly because of the clog. That’s why you felt low on energy. We’ll restart them slowly now that the tube is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we checked your blood sugar earlier—it was low. That explains the weakness. Once feeds restart, you should feel stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fever… earlier?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had a mild fever in the ER. Because you have a Foley catheter, we thought it might be a UTI, so they started an antibiotic just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Antibiotic? Again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know you’ve had C. diff before, so we’re being careful. The urine test wasn’t strongly positive, and you don’t have other signs of infection—no confusion, no high white count. So we’re stopping the antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good… don’t want stomach issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. But because you got an antibiotic, we’re restarting your oral vancomycin for a week—just to prevent C. diff from coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m checking in after your first night. The nursing team unclogged the J-port again yesterday, but they got it working with flushing. No replacement needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah… keeps clogging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re figuring that out. From now on, medications will go through the G-port, and feeds through the J-port. And flush both after each use. That should help prevent clogs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Flush more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll make sure the nursing home gets clear instructions. We’re also checking your blood sugar four times a day for the next few days, since you had a low one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… don’t want that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray came back. It shows your usual lung changes from COPD—no new pneumonia. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cough… still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s likely from secretions and your trach. We’re continuing your albuterol nebs and glycopyrrolate to keep things clear. No need for more antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good… tired of meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs are stable. Liver tests are slightly off—ALT is 51—but that’s been up before. Nothing urgent, but your team might check it later as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Liver? HIV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but your HIV regimen—Darunavir, Ritonavir, Truvada—is staying the same. Your last CD4 was 178, so we’re keeping you on atovaquone for PCP prevention too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… still protected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And we’re continuing your Keppra for seizures, omeprazole for reflux, and Creon for digestion—all as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Rash?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still treating the back rash with the cream and powder. And we noticed a small stage 1 pressure sore on your sacrum. We’ll keep turning you and use a special pad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Need to move more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re bedbound, so we rely on staff to reposition you. The nursing home will continue that. We’re also keeping you NPO by mouth—feeds only through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your Foley catheter was changed yesterday. Since you had urinary retention before, we want to keep it in until your urology appointment. They’ll do more tests soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Catheter… okay. Urology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, outpatient urodynamic testing is scheduled. They’ll check how your bladder works and decide next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go back to the nursing home today. Your tube is working well, no more fevers, and you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great… thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending detailed instructions: meds in G-tube, feeds in J-tube, flush both. Check blood sugar four times daily for three days. Finish the oral vancomycin for C. diff prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Keep doing what works.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep up with your trach care, nebs, and turning. Call if the tube clogs again or you feel unwell. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with advanced HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, tracheostomy, and GJ tube dependence was admitted from a skilled nursing facility due to a malfunctioning feeding tube and an isolated fever. The GJ tube was successfully unclogged at the bedside without replacement, and tube feeds were restarted, resolving a transient episode of hypoglycemia. The fever was attributed to catheter colonization rather than active infection, so antibiotics were withheld after initial empiric treatment. He remained afebrile, with stable labs and no signs of pneumonia on chest imaging. His chronic conditions, including seizures, pancreatic insufficiency, GERD, and depression, were managed with continued home medications. A stage 1 sacral pressure ulcer was noted, and preventive measures were reinforced. He completed a short course of oral vancomycin for C. diff prophylaxis after antibiotic exposure and was discharged back to the facility with detailed instructions on tube management, blood sugar monitoring, and follow-up with urology for ongoing urinary retention.
